tip: 'Je viens de finir' means 'I just finished' – venir de + verb is French's recent past. It reads literally as 'I come from finishing', yet the plain present does past-tense work here.
French has no '-ing' tense. To pin an action to right now, wrap it in 'être en train de': 'est en train d'atterrir' = is in the middle of landing this very second.
'Laisser tomber' is literally 'to let fall', but it means to drop or quit: 'a laissé tomber ses études' = gave up his studies. Also how you say you ditched someone.
'Finir par' isn't about finishing – it means to end up doing something eventually: 'vont finir par accepter' = they'll come around to accepting in the end.
'Faillir' + verb means to nearly do something: 'avait failli avoir un accident' = had almost had a crash. This verb basically only lives in past tenses.
'Se faire avoir' is literally 'to get oneself had' – the set phrase for being tricked or scammed: 'je me suis fait avoir' = I got taken in, I fell for it.
'Bien que' (although) always forces the subjunctive: 'bien que le temps fût'. That 'fût' is the literary imperfect subjunctive of être – in speech you'd just say 'soit'.
